passages.title: Vashti refuses the king
passages.summary: Ahasuerus holds large feasts. Vashti refuses his order to appear. Memucan urges him to replace her.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson starts with the decision to replace Vashti. How do the advisers turn one refusal into rules for wives?

contextNote.title: A court turns one refusal into a household rule
contextNote.text: The advisers treat Vashti's refusal as a threat beyond the palace. Their proposed response extends royal authority into every household. The many languages of the letters enlarge one court conflict into a royal order. That pattern prepares readers for the later letters against the Jews.

passages.title: Esther becomes queen
passages.summary: Hegai helps Esther in the women’s house. Ahasuerus chooses her as queen. Mordecai reports a plot against him.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem and Babylon belong to the earlier family account. The palace story takes place in Susa.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Mordecai’s care for Esther. How does he help her after she becomes queen?

contextNote.title: Access to the court does not equal freedom
contextNote.text: Esther gains favor while keeping her family identity concealed. The account follows preparation, selection, and commands within the women's house. Royal preference shapes the choices available to its residents. Mordecai's recorded service adds a second hidden fact that will later change the court.

passages.title: Haman orders the Jews’ deaths
passages.summary: Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman. Haman obtains the king’s ring and sends orders to kill all the Jews.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Haman’s anger. How does his anger at Mordecai threaten all the Jews?

contextNote.title: A written order carries danger across distance
contextNote.text: The threat travels through officials, languages, letters, and the royal seal. A court decision can reach households far from the palace. Haman turns local hatred into an order for mass killing. The story makes the machinery of rule part of the danger. Authority must be answered at that same public level.

passages.title: Esther decides to approach the king
passages.summary: Hathach carries messages between Mordecai and Esther. Esther asks the Jews to fast before she risks approaching the king.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies courage and fasting. What help does Esther ask for before approaching the king?

contextNote.title: The palace cannot separate one person from a threatened people
contextNote.text: Mordecai warns that the royal house cannot guarantee Esther's safety. Her hidden identity now becomes a claim on her action. She answers with a shared fast before taking a personal risk. The exchange changes her from a selected queen into a public advocate.

passages.title: Two invitations and Haman’s anger
passages.summary: The king receives Esther. She invites him and Haman to two meals. Zeresh suggests preparing a gallows for Mordecai.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares Esther’s risk with Haman’s pride. Why do his honors fail to satisfy him?

contextNote.title: Honor does not satisfy a demand for submission
contextNote.text: Haman lists wealth, family, and royal favor before dismissing them as insufficient. One man's refusal to bow outweighs all those honors for him. Esther's delayed request builds tension while he prepares violence. The chapter exposes how status can increase rather than settle resentment.

passages.title: Haman must honor Mordecai
passages.summary: The king hears how Mordecai saved him. Haman must lead Mordecai through the city with royal clothing and a horse.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson recalls the king’s records. How does the saved report change Mordecai’s treatment?

contextNote.title: An unread reward becomes the turning point
contextNote.text: A sleepless king asks for records of earlier service. Mordecai’s forgotten act suddenly gains value at court. Haman arrives with a different purpose and loses control of the scene. The reversal grows from timing, memory, and mistaken expectation. The book lets ordinary court routines carry extraordinary consequences.

passages.title: Esther names Haman as the enemy
passages.summary: Esther asks for her life and her people’s lives. She names Haman. Harbonah points out the gallows, and Haman dies.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Haman’s choices and their results. How does Esther explain the danger to the king?

contextNote.title: Esther gives the policy a face the king recognizes
contextNote.text: Her appeal begins with her own life before naming the danger to her people. The king must confront the consequence of an order bearing his authority. Haman's collapse comes through the court's sudden change of favor. That reversal does not yet remove the written threat.

passages.title: New orders allow the Jews to fight
passages.summary: Esther asks again for her people. Mordecai receives the king’s ring. New letters permit the Jews to gather and fight attackers.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies fasting during danger. Why must Esther keep asking for help after Haman dies?

contextNote.title: A new letter must answer an existing order
contextNote.text: The king's explanation limits what can happen to a sealed decree. Esther's success therefore requires further writing, messengers, and permission to gather. Killing Haman has not removed the machinery he used. The threatened people need protection that reaches beyond the palace.

passages.title: Victory, violence, and Purim
passages.summary: The Jews kill their enemies without taking goods. Esther requests another day in Susa. Letters establish Purim with feasts and gifts.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Esther’s courage with later joy. How do gifts help people remember the rescue?

contextNote.title: A festival keeps both grief and survival in memory
contextNote.text: The festival marks a change from mourning to joy. Gifts to poor people make relief a shared practice. The preceding violence remains part of the account. The ending explains how later readers can remember deliverance together. Celebration here includes food, records, and duties toward others.

passages.title: Mordecai serves his people
passages.summary: Ahasuerus collects payment from his lands. Mordecai holds high office and works for his people’s good.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Mordecai works for his people’s good. Who benefits from the power he receives?

contextNote.title: High office receives a measure beyond personal honor
contextNote.text: The ending places Mordecai's rank beside his work for his people. His importance depends on seeking their welfare and speaking for them. The brief return to royal taxes also preserves the setting of foreign rule. Survival has changed access to power without ending the empire.
